speaker: Rudyard Griffiths
text: Ladies and gentlemen, welcome to the Munk Debate on the global refugee crisis.

speaker: Rudyard Griffiths
text: My name is Rudyard Griffiths and I have the privilege of organizing this semi-annual debate series and, once again, serving as your moderator.

speaker: Rudyard Griffiths
text: I want to begin tonight’s proceedings by welcoming the North America–wide TV audience that is tuning in to this debate right now across Canada from coast to coast to coast on CPAC, Canada’s Public Affairs Channel, and across the continental United States on C-SPAN.

speaker: Rudyard Griffiths
text: It’s the first time the Munk Debate has been live throughout the continent of North America and it’s terrific to have that viewing audience joining us this evening.

speaker: Rudyard Griffiths
text: A warm hello also to our online audience.

speaker: Rudyard Griffiths
text: They’re logging onto this debate right now on our website, www.munkdebates.com .

speaker: Rudyard Griffiths
text: It’s great to have you as virtual participants in tonight’s proceedings.

speaker: Rudyard Griffiths
text: And finally, hello to you, the more than three thousand people who’ve once again filled Roy Thomson Hall on a Friday night to capacity for yet another Munk Debate.

speaker: Rudyard Griffiths
text: All of us associated with the Aurea Foundation thank you for supporting the simple idea that this debate series is dedicated to: more and better public debates.

speaker: Rudyard Griffiths
text: So, bravo, ladies and gentlemen.

speaker: Rudyard Griffiths
text: Thank you for being part of tonight’s conversation.

speaker: Rudyard Griffiths
text: Our ability to continue these debates year after year, and to bring some of the world’s sharpest minds and brightest thinkers here to the stage, would not be possible without the generosity, the foresight, and the creativity of our hosts tonight.

speaker: Rudyard Griffiths
text: Please join me in a warm appreciation of the Aurea Foundation and its founders, Peter and Melanie Munk.

speaker: Rudyard Griffiths
text: It’s the moment we’ve been waiting for.

speaker: Rudyard Griffiths
text: Let’s get our two teams of debaters out here centre stage and our debate underway.

speaker: Rudyard Griffiths
text: Our resolution tonight is taken from the inscription on the Statue of Liberty, “Be it resolved: Give us your tired, your poor, your huddled masses yearning to breathe free.”

speaker: Rudyard Griffiths
text: Please welcome our first speaker in support of the resolution.

speaker: Rudyard Griffiths
text: She’s a former Canadian Supreme Court justice, chief prosecutor of the International Criminal Tribunals for Yugoslavia and Rwanda, and the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights (UNHCR), among many other accomplishments.

speaker: Rudyard Griffiths
text: Ladies and gentlemen, please welcome Canada’s Louise Arbour.

speaker: Rudyard Griffiths
text: Louise’s teammate is the internationally acclaimed historian, cultural commentator, and art critic Simon Schama.

speaker: Rudyard Griffiths
text: Please come out on stage, Simon.

speaker: Rudyard Griffiths
text: Well, one great team of debaters deserves another.

speaker: Rudyard Griffiths
text: Speaking against the resolution, “Be it resolved: Give us your tired, your poor, your huddled masses yearning to breathe free,” is the renowned columnist, author, and conservative human rights activist Mark Steyn.

speaker: Rudyard Griffiths
text: Mark’s debating partner is the leader of UKIP, the United Kingdom Independence Party, and a member of the European Parliament.

speaker: Rudyard Griffiths
text: He’s here tonight from the United Kingdom.

speaker: Rudyard Griffiths
text: Under his leadership, UKIP won almost four million votes in the 2015 national election.

speaker: Rudyard Griffiths
text: Ladies and gentlemen, Nigel Farage.

speaker: Rudyard Griffiths
text: Before our debate begins, I need your help with a last-minute housekeeping item: our countdown clock, an invention we love at the Munk Debates.

speaker: Rudyard Griffiths
text: It keeps us on schedule and our debaters on their toes.

speaker: Rudyard Griffiths
text: When you see these clocks reach their final moments, join me in a round of applause that will let our debaters know that their time is up.

speaker: Rudyard Griffiths
text: We had Henry Kissinger up here once and he didn’t think his time was up … but I digress.

speaker: Rudyard Griffiths
text: I don’t think any of our debaters will make the same mistake.

speaker: Rudyard Griffiths
text: Now, this is the part I enjoy most.

speaker: Rudyard Griffiths
text: We asked all of you here tonight to vote on the resolution on your way in.

speaker: Rudyard Griffiths
text: You were asked, “Do you support or oppose the motion, ‘Be it resolved: give us your tired, your poor, your huddled masses yearning to breathe free’?”

speaker: Rudyard Griffiths
text: The results are interesting: 77 percent of you agree, and 23 percent disagree.

speaker: Rudyard Griffiths
text: To give a sense of how much this debate is in play, we asked: “Depending on what you hear during the debate, are you open to changing your votes?”

speaker: Rudyard Griffiths
text: Let’s see that result.

speaker: Rudyard Griffiths
text: Wow: 79 percent of you were open to changing your votes.

speaker: Rudyard Griffiths
text: Only 21 percent of you are committed to your viewpoint.

speaker: Rudyard Griffiths
text: This debate is very much in play; either side can take it.

speaker: Rudyard Griffiths
text: Let’s go to our opening statements.

speaker: Rudyard Griffiths
text: I’d like six minutes on the clock for each of our debaters.

speaker: Rudyard Griffiths
text: Ms. Arbour, your six minutes begins now.

speaker: Louise Arbour
text: Thank you very much.

speaker: Louise Arbour
text: Good evening, ladies and gentlemen.

speaker: Louise Arbour
text: The words of the motion that I’m here to support were written by a woman, Emma Lazarus, and these words are engraved on a famous statute of a woman holding a torch, and maybe less noticeably holding also the tablets of law with a broken chain at her feet.

speaker: Louise Arbour
text: So it should come as no surprise to you that this has considerable appeal to me.

speaker: Louise Arbour
text: But don’t let that fool you.

speaker: Louise Arbour
text: This is not a sentimental call for do-gooders to unite, nor a romantic projection of what the new world is going to be all about.

speaker: Louise Arbour
text: Understood in today’s terms, it’s a moving, poetic way of capturing both the spirit and the letter of the 1951 Refugee Convention.

speaker: Louise Arbour
text: It was written essentially because of and for Europe, and it remains the framework within which a world purporting to be governed by the rule of law must deal with the current refugee crisis in Europe and must also stop turning a blind eye to equally pressing crises elsewhere — in South Sudan, for instance.

speaker: Louise Arbour
text: This is part of the “Never again!” that the world screamed loud and clear after the Holocaust and has betrayed on so many occasions since then.

speaker: Louise Arbour
text: Today should not be one of those.

speaker: Louise Arbour
text: I want to look at this issue both from a Canadian and international perspective.

speaker: Louise Arbour
text: The international framework is very clear.

speaker: Louise Arbour
text: Virtually all of the countries concerned with the current flow of refugees fleeing the war-torn countries of Syria, Iraq, Afghanistan, Somalia, and Libya are parties to the Refugee Convention, and they are obligated to grant asylum to those fleeing political and other forms of persecution.

speaker: Louise Arbour
text: The protection framework that is set in place by the convention outlines that refugees should not be penalized for their illegal entry or stay in a country.

speaker: Louise Arbour
text: The reverse would obviously be a way to completely emasculate the right of asylum, and the principle of non-refoulement precludes returning refugees to countries where they are at risk.

speaker: Louise Arbour
text: This puts a disproportionate demand on countries that are more easily reachable than others.

speaker: Louise Arbour
text: In the case of Syria, the neighbouring countries of Lebanon, Jordan, and Turkey currently have some 4.5 million Syrian refugees, and the countries that are at the external borders of Europe — Greece, Italy, and so on — are also seeing a large influx.

speaker: Louise Arbour
text: This leads to another fundamental principle that underpins the Refugee Convention: the need for international co-operation and burden sharing, and I’m cautious here about using the word burden .

speaker: Louise Arbour
text: Now I want to mention Canada.

speaker: Louise Arbour
text: We often define ourselves by our geography, and on this issue our geography is relevant.

speaker: Louise Arbour
text: The nature of our borders is such that we are virtually immune from a flow of asylum seekers arriving on our soil by land or sea — although, the result of the upcoming American elections may change that!

speaker: Louise Arbour
text: We’ll cross that bridge when we get there.

speaker: Louise Arbour
text: As a result, I believe we have a special obligation to provide for a generous resettlement program aiming both at welcoming refugees and at easing the burden on states that are struggling to live up to their international obligations.

speaker: Louise Arbour
text: And I believe that with true international co-operation in place, this is eminently feasible.

speaker: Louise Arbour
text: We should do it the smart way by ensuring that asylum seekers can travel safely to places of refuge, thereby undercutting the smugglers, and by deploying extraordinary resources to meet this extraordinary challenge.

speaker: Louise Arbour
text: I am aware of the fear that an influx of foreigners will transform our social fabric in an undesirable way, but the reality is that our social fabric is changing anyway in this increasingly interconnected world.

speaker: Louise Arbour
text: We have a choice.

speaker: Louise Arbour
text: We can look to the past and stagnate in isolation, or we can embrace a future in which our children will develop their own culture fully open to that of others, inspired by the choices that we are making today.

speaker: Louise Arbour
text: The greatest threat to Western values is not an influx of people who may not share those values today; it’s the hypocrisy of those claiming to protect these values and then repudiating them by their actions.

speaker: Louise Arbour
text: I expect that we’re going to hear tonight that Muslims are different, that they pose a unique, novel, and existential threat to our democracies.

speaker: Louise Arbour
text: Not only has this been the ugly response to just about every wave of new immigrants in history, but, ironically, it plays right into the hands of the violent jihadist groups that are attacking us.

speaker: Louise Arbour
text: These violent groups have a political, not a religious agenda.

speaker: Louise Arbour
text: They seek to destroy our democracies not by infiltrating or taking over our institutions but by letting us slowly self-implode in response to the fear that risks turning us against ourselves, thereby destroying the very key features of our open society.

speaker: Louise Arbour
text: We need to be smarter than that, and we need to welcome people who, like all of us who came from somewhere else at some point, will build an ever-evolving free and strong Canada.

speaker: Louise Arbour
text: Thank you very much.

speaker: Rudyard Griffiths
text: With time still on the clock.

speaker: Rudyard Griffiths
text: Mark Steyn, you’re up next.

speaker: Rudyard Griffiths
text: Your six minutes begins now.

speaker: Mark Steyn
text: Madame Arbour described a refugee situation that is not happening in Europe at the moment.

speaker: Mark Steyn
text: The great question before us tonight is whether the “huddled masses” on those “teeming shores” are really “yearning to breathe free,” or whether they’re simply economic migrants who want to avail themselves of the comforts of advanced societies.

speaker: Mark Steyn
text: There are three thousand people here in Roy Thomson Hall tonight.

speaker: Mark Steyn
text: It would nice if everyone who lived in Toronto could be in Roy Thomson Hall right now, but if everyone in Toronto moves into Roy Thomson Hall, it isn’t Roy Thomson Hall anymore.

speaker: Mark Steyn
text: And that’s the situation facing Europe today.

speaker: Mark Steyn
text: The people who have entered Europe are not refugees as the term has traditionally been understood and as Madame Arbour explained in terms of the Geneva Convention.

speaker: Mark Steyn
text: In Europe in 2015, men represented 77 percent of the asylum applications — that’s an extraordinary population deformation.

speaker: Mark Steyn
text: In most civil wars, this is the demographic that would be back home fighting for their country.

speaker: Mark Steyn
text: It’s as if, during the American Revolution, General Washington and the rest of the chaps had gone off to France and left Martha and the other women and children back home to fend for themselves.

speaker: Mark Steyn
text: What does it mean to breathe free?

speaker: Mark Steyn
text: Under the Taliban, it’s illegal for Madame Arbour to feel sunlight on her face.

speaker: Mark Steyn
text: It’s literally a crime for her to “breathe free.”

speaker: Mark Steyn
text: She can breathe only through a mask approved by the man who owns her, in effect.

speaker: Mark Steyn
text: So what happens when you put a man from that kind of society in, say, a Scandinavian town?

speaker: Mark Steyn
text: Northern Europe has enjoyed a culture of mixed public bathing since the nineteenth century, but a benign social activity to Germans and Scandinavians is something entirely different to men from a culture where women are chattel.

speaker: Mark Steyn
text: Female patrons of public baths are now routinely assaulted.

speaker: Mark Steyn
text: And in January, Sweden’s national swimming arena was forced to segregate men and women in the hot tubs for the first time.

speaker: Mark Steyn
text: Goodbye to a century-old tradition; migrant rights trump your culture.

speaker: Mark Steyn
text: Our response is, “Oh, they come from a different culture; they don’t know that you’re not meant to grope women’s breasts.”

speaker: Mark Steyn
text: In Germany they put up pictograms with a breast and a groping hand with a red X through it.

speaker: Mark Steyn
text: Last month, a mere fortnight after acing a training course on how to treat women with respect, a fifteen-year-old Afghan dragged a caterer at a Belgian refugee centre into the basement and raped her.

speaker: Mark Steyn
text: We’ll say that the course on treating women with respect needs some fine-tuning.

speaker: Mark Steyn
text: We’ll get better pictograms.

speaker: Mark Steyn
text: But in the meantime, migrant rights trump women’s rights.

speaker: Mark Steyn
text: Madame Arbour was the first prosecutor ever to charge rape as a crime against humanity.

speaker: Mark Steyn
text: In 2007 she published an important report on the use of rape in Sudan as a weapon of war.

speaker: Mark Steyn
text: It was a distressing report.

speaker: Mark Steyn
text: She documented fifteen individual cases of sexual assault, including rape, in victims as young as fourteen.

speaker: Mark Steyn
text: If Madame Arbour were to publish a similar report on Germany today, she’d be able to cite more than five hundred cases from just one night in just one town — Cologne — on New Year’s Eve.

speaker: Mark Steyn
text: Victims were as young as three.

speaker: Mark Steyn
text: Think about that: a three-year-old was raped by a migrant.

speaker: Mark Steyn
text: A seven-year-old was gang-raped by five migrants in Hamburg just a few days ago.

speaker: Mark Steyn
text: On Wednesday, a schoolgirl was gang-raped on the ferry from Sweden to Finland.

speaker: Mark Steyn
text: Migrant rights now trump children’s rights.

speaker: Mark Steyn
text: What a pity Madame Arbour’s successor at the UN isn’t interested in producing a report on that rape epidemic.

speaker: Mark Steyn
text: The police chief of Vienna has advised women that it’s no longer safe to go out unaccompanied.

speaker: Mark Steyn
text: Migrant rights trump the right to freedom of movement.

speaker: Mark Steyn
text: It’s easy to shrug — “Oh, well, it’s just a few disabled kids, just anecdotes.”

speaker: Mark Steyn
text: Forget the anecdotes and run the numbers.

speaker: Mark Steyn
text: In Europe, unaccompanied minors are 90 percent male, which means that in one year, Swedish adolescents now have a more distorted sex differential than China does after thirty years of its totalitarian one-child policy.

speaker: Mark Steyn
text: In China there are 119 boys for every girl.

speaker: Mark Steyn
text: Among Swedish adolescents, it is now 123 boys for every girl, just from last year’s immigration.

speaker: Mark Steyn
text: That’s a fact.

speaker: Mark Steyn
text: I hope tonight we’ll put aside the sentimentalism that often imbues this subject and stick with the facts.

speaker: Mark Steyn
text: Madame Arbour said some things that I agree with.

speaker: Mark Steyn
text: She recently said, “Why are we always talking about the danger that these people will transform us? They may transform us for the better.”

speaker: Mark Steyn
text: So she and I agree that immigration on this scale is transformative.

speaker: Mark Steyn
text: The only difference is that Madame Arbour thinks it’s for the better and I don’t.

speaker: Mark Steyn
text: I’m genuinely curious to know what aspects of Afghan and Syrian and Sudanese culture she would like us to be transformed by: Women’s rights?

speaker: Mark Steyn
text: Fast-track justice whereby gays get thrown off rooftops?

speaker: Mark Steyn
text: Polygamy?

speaker: Mark Steyn
text: Child brides?

speaker: Mark Steyn
text: Clitoridectomies?

speaker: Mark Steyn
text: The bracing commitment to free speech?

speaker: Mark Steyn
text: I would like an answer on that from Madame Arbour tonight.

speaker: Mark Steyn
text: Thank you very much.

speaker: Rudyard Griffiths
text: Simon Schama, over to you.

speaker: Simon Schama
text: Well, I’m going to start by saying, “Oh Canada, your borders are safe.”

speaker: Simon Schama
text: I can tell you why.

speaker: Simon Schama
text: I was asked this morning at the Toronto airport what I was doing here, and I said, “Well, I’ve come to talk about refugees and migrants,” and I was immediately taken off for secondary screening.

speaker: Simon Schama
text: So it’s not only dangerous to talk about it; it’s dangerous to be known to be talking about it.

speaker: Simon Schama
text: The words in our resolution tonight were written by Emma Lazarus.

speaker: Simon Schama
text: She was a Sephardic Jewess and a wealthy woman in New York.

speaker: Simon Schama
text: She wrote them in 1883 after looking at the victims of Russian pogroms who had come to America having suffered horrendous atrocities in Kishinev, Odessa, and Elisavetgrad.

speaker: Simon Schama
text: She saw them on Wards Island, and she didn’t make the distinction that they were economic migrants.

speaker: Simon Schama
text: By the way, Mark, your number is wrong.

speaker: Simon Schama
text: It’s not 77 percent; we know from United Nations agencies that the figure is 61 percent, and that’s significant.

speaker: Simon Schama
text: This is an uninterrupted moment, Mark; we’ll have rebuttal time afterwards.

speaker: Simon Schama
text: I know radio hosts don’t usually like that, but that’s the case.

speaker: Simon Schama
text: She did that because when you are fleeing from a place of cruelty and atrocity and your house has been blown up, your whole possibility of livelihood’s been taken away from you, and your children have no food, no medicine, what are you exactly?

speaker: Simon Schama
text: You’re terrifyingly running away from catastrophe, and vast numbers of Syrians are displaced — four million of them internally displaced.

speaker: Simon Schama
text: So those who are escaping the hell of Libya and Somalia and Afghanistan are fleeing exactly the monsters of Islamofascism that Mark accurately describes.

speaker: Simon Schama
text: They’re not their friends.

speaker: Simon Schama
text: They’re not their secret co-conspirators.

speaker: Simon Schama
text: They are horrified.

speaker: Simon Schama
text: They’re trying to get away from that culture.

speaker: Simon Schama
text: Now, it’s fine to say, “Well, in those days …”

speaker: Simon Schama
text: And as some of you know, the reason why the lines from Emma Lazarus’s “The New Colossus” were not immediately put on the Statue of Liberty — they were only put there in 1903 as a result of the efforts of her friend Georgina Schuyler — was because of a ferocious agitation on the part of some people at the immigration restriction league and its British equivalent, called the British Brothers’ League.

speaker: Simon Schama
text: These groups said the unwashed, the filthy, those who do not share our language, our religion, our values would destroy the white race.

speaker: Simon Schama
text: Madison Grant wrote a book called The Passing of the Great Race .

speaker: Simon Schama
text: Tom Watson, the populist, described the millions of distressed as the scum of creation.

speaker: Simon Schama
text: Nonetheless, the United States, as an honour to its tradition set out in Crèvecoeur’s “What Is an American” in 1782, admitted five million of those refugees between 1880 and 1890.

speaker: Simon Schama
text: And the argument will be made that in those days democracy was more confident.

speaker: Simon Schama
text: I agree with you absolutely about that.

speaker: Simon Schama
text: It was.

speaker: Simon Schama
text: It was more articulate.

speaker: Simon Schama
text: It was less offensive.

speaker: Simon Schama
text: It was more forthright.

speaker: Simon Schama
text: And besides, you may say, people coming from eastern Europe or central Europe did not bear democracy the grudge; they didn’t want to overthrow it.

speaker: Simon Schama
text: Yes, they did.

speaker: Simon Schama
text: Yes, they did.

speaker: Simon Schama
text: Those teeming millions that Emma Lazarus emotionally described were full of anarchists and communists dedicated to the overthrow of capitalism.

speaker: Simon Schama
text: But liberal capitalism was strong enough to let them in anyway, and as a result, the American Republic and Great Britain thrived and flourished and prospered, and my own grandparents were among those who had Britain to thank for that more expansive view of what democracy could accommodate.

speaker: Simon Schama
text: Right now, we’re talking about a drop in the ocean, really.

speaker: Simon Schama
text: There are one billion of us in Europe and Canada and the United States.

speaker: Simon Schama
text: We’re talking about 20,000 refugees being admitted to Britain.

speaker: Simon Schama
text: We’re talking about 100,000 refugees in the United States proposed by the president, of whom only 25,000 will come from Syria.

speaker: Simon Schama
text: Are they all ravening sexual monsters of Mark Steyn’s X-rated horror?

speaker: Simon Schama
text: Muslims are not all Salafists.

speaker: Simon Schama
text: And not all Salafists are jihadists either.

speaker: Simon Schama
text: There are quieter Salafists.

speaker: Simon Schama
text: Do Salafist jihadists pose a mortal threat?

speaker: Simon Schama
text: You bet your life they do.

speaker: Simon Schama
text: There is a real war of that kind going on, but what should we do to resist the poison of apocalyptic millenarians?

speaker: Simon Schama
text: The answer is not to demonize all Muslims but to engage with them.

speaker: Simon Schama
text: And we say, “Well, who are we engaging with? There are no Muslims who really want to stand up.”

speaker: Simon Schama
text: That is not true.

speaker: Simon Schama
text: After the attack both in Paris and Brussels, 150 imams in New York got up and made a statement about the abhorrence of the act.

speaker: Simon Schama
text: There are even Koranic scholars, the greatest of whom is Javed Ahmad Ghamidi — if you don’t know his work look it up — who are absolutely dedicated to denouncing jihadism as a perversion of the Koran.

speaker: Simon Schama
text: And I just want to say that it can’t possibly be true that you can’t have a pluralist Muslim adoption of Western norms.

speaker: Simon Schama
text: In Britain, Nigel, we lived with that for years and years before jihadism became the monstrosity that it is now.

speaker: Simon Schama
text: My green grocer is a Kurdish Muslim.

speaker: Simon Schama
text: We turn on the radio in the morning and you hear Razia Iqbal through the BBC.

speaker: Simon Schama
text: My local newsagent tells me when to look at the Jewish Chronicle , and his name is Ahmed.

speaker: Rudyard Griffiths
text: Nigel.

speaker: Nigel Farage
text: Good evening, everybody.

speaker: Nigel Farage
text: If we’re going to discuss the global refugee crisis, we’d better use the European Union (EU) as a case study.

speaker: Nigel Farage
text: But first we must start by asking ourselves: What is a refugee?

speaker: Nigel Farage
text: Now, I speak here today as the child of a family of refugees.

speaker: Nigel Farage
text: We were French Protestants being burned at the stake for our political opinions — something many in Westminster would perhaps like to bring back today.

speaker: Nigel Farage
text: There is no country in Europe that needs lectures about looking after refugees.

speaker: Nigel Farage
text: But I come from a country that has, I think, done it better than anybody else.

speaker: Nigel Farage
text: The Brits have done it with Jewish people.

speaker: Nigel Farage
text: We’ve done it with Ugandan Asians.

speaker: Nigel Farage
text: But what is a refugee?

speaker: Nigel Farage
text: According to this 1951 convention that we talked about earlier, it’s a person with a well-founded fear of persecution because of race, religion, political opinions, or orientation, who is outside their own country and fears returning to it.

speaker: Nigel Farage
text: I know it’s tempting to support this motion.

speaker: Nigel Farage
text: It sounds wonderful — “Give us your poor, your weak, your huddled masses” — and in doing so we can perhaps feel a sense of our own moral superiority.

speaker: Nigel Farage
text: But just look where that idea has got the EU in the course of the last year.

speaker: Nigel Farage
text: Jean-Claude Juncker, the unelected European Commission president who, I have to say after a good lunch, is rather fun to be with — particularly if I’ve been with him, actually — has changed the definition of what a refugee is to include people who come from war-torn areas.

speaker: Nigel Farage
text: Given that the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees says there are currently fifty-nine million people displaced in the world, that’s quite a big number.

speaker: Nigel Farage
text: But Juncker has taken an even broader definition.

speaker: Nigel Farage
text: He said that you could qualify as a European refugee if you come from extreme poverty, which would mean three billion people could potentially come to Europe.

speaker: Nigel Farage
text: All of this was massively compounded by Chancellor Angela Merkel, who effectively did say “give us your weak and your poor and your huddled masses” in what I think has proved to be the worst foreign policy decision in Europe since 1945.

speaker: Nigel Farage
text: In my view, her moral superiority was based on a level of war guilt that still exists in Germany.

speaker: Nigel Farage
text: But she opened up the doors and a million people came in last year.

speaker: Nigel Farage
text: But virtually none of them would qualify as refugees on any classical definition.

speaker: Nigel Farage
text: And in fact, most of them were somewhat aggressive young males who, when they arrived and got through the border, punched the air and chanted like football supporters.

speaker: Nigel Farage
text: I remember as a young man watching the BBC and seeing Ugandan Asians landing on the tarmac at Heathrow, humbled, thankful, and promising that they would repay the debt Britain had shown them by integrating and becoming part of our society.

speaker: Nigel Farage
text: Sadly, that is not what has happened in this case.

speaker: Nigel Farage
text: Nobody on this side of the argument is trying to say that Islam is bad or that all Muslims are bad.

speaker: Nigel Farage
text: But what we are saying is that if you allow a very large number of young males to come to European countries, and if they come from a culture where women are at best second-class citizens, don’t be surprised to see abominations such as the one we saw outside the Cologne train station on New Year’s Eve.

speaker: Nigel Farage
text: And don’t be surprised that the formerly rather sleepy Swedish city of Malmö has now become the rape capital of Europe.

speaker: Nigel Farage
text: But that is nothing compared to what the boss of Europol said three weeks ago.

speaker: Nigel Farage
text: He said there are now five thousand jihadi fighters, every one of them potentially a terrorist, who have got into Europe through the Greek islands posing as migrants.

speaker: Nigel Farage
text: When the Islamic State of Iraq and the Levant (ISIL) says they will use the migrant routes to destroy the civilization of Europe, I suggest we start to take them seriously.

speaker: Nigel Farage
text: And the difference between what is going on now and any other either migratory or refugee wave in the history of humankind that I can see is that never before have we had a fifth column — albeit a small one, thank God — but a fifth column living within our own communities that hates us, wants to kill us, and wants to completely overturn our way of life.

speaker: Nigel Farage
text: I believe that we in the West should give people refugee status.

speaker: Nigel Farage
text: Throughout this whole tragedy in the Middle East and North Africa, not one person in a serious level of politics has dared to speak up for the Christians — the Christians in Iraq and the Christians in Syria, who are now only 10 percent of what they were just a few years ago.

speaker: Nigel Farage
text: They qualify for refugee status because they’re being persecuted for who they are.

speaker: Nigel Farage
text: We have to oppose this motion, which is at best impractical and at worst poses a threat to our entire way of life.

speaker: Nigel Farage
text: I want us to have a proper processing mechanism.

speaker: Nigel Farage
text: I want us to do all the things we’ve done, as Brits particularly, over centuries.

speaker: Nigel Farage

text: When you’ve got second- and third-generation Belgians, Frenchmen, Germans, Britons, and Canadians going off to join ISIL, blowing up Paris, blowing up Brussels, that should foster a certain modesty among us that our skills at assimilation are not as awesome and all-encompassing as they were in the nineteenth century.

speaker: Mark Steyn
text: And to think, the response is to suddenly accelerate immigration from the same source?

speaker: Mark Steyn
text: It’s very bizarre.

speaker: Mark Steyn
text: In what sense are these people Belgian?

speaker: Simon Schama
text: In what sense is Razia Iqbal British?

speaker: Simon Schama
text: She’s fully British, right?

speaker: Nigel Farage
text: Yes, she’s fully British.

speaker: Simon Schama
text: And she happens to be a British Muslim, right?

speaker: Simon Schama
text: And how much more British can you get than doing the BBC World Service?

speaker: Mark Steyn
text: Yes.

speaker: Mark Steyn
text: I work with Zeinab Badawi at Channel 4 in Britain.

speaker: Mark Steyn
text: I’ve got no problem with that.

speaker: Mark Steyn
text: But that’s my point.

speaker: Mark Steyn
text: Holding a passport does not make you Canadian.

speaker: Mark Steyn
text: It does not make you Belgian and does not make you French.

speaker: Louise Arbour
text: What?

speaker: Simon Schama
text: I agree.

speaker: Simon Schama
text: I think this is the difference between us, actually.

speaker: Simon Schama
text: There are those of us who are possibly naively optimistic humanists, who think it is not impossible to be an orthodox Muslim and a good Canadian or a good Brit, and a good democrat at the same time.

speaker: Simon Schama
text: And for that you need to be involved and engaged in exercises of civic education, which make it clear that you can indeed go to a mosque for Friday prayers and still be a decent, democratically participating citizen.

speaker: Simon Schama
text: And I don’t think this has actually happened.

speaker: Simon Schama
text: If you go to the mosque and the imam happens to preach the destruction of the society that you’re living in, bloody well turn him in.

speaker: Simon Schama
text: Turn him in!

speaker: Rudyard Griffiths
text: Mark, do you want to respond?

speaker: Mark Steyn
text: That doesn’t happen, unfortunately.

speaker: Mark Steyn
text: If you look at the RCMP statistics of radicalized mosques you’ll understand that all over this city and Montreal and Calgary and Edmonton and Vancouver there are any number of radicalized mosques where people just sit on their hands.

speaker: Mark Steyn
text: I go back to my point, Simon — you have to have something for migrants to assimilate with.

speaker: Simon Schama
text: Yes.

speaker: Mark Steyn
text: The people in British schools haven’t a clue about most of the history you know.

speaker: Mark Steyn
text: They don’t teach history in North American schools.

speaker: Mark Steyn
text: My kids are in some school where it’s called Social Studies and they do a little bit of it and it’s always the same thing.

speaker: Mark Steyn
text: Martin Luther King comes round like the Number 23 bus.

speaker: Simon Schama
text: I actually have a movement to abolish the term now.

speaker: Mark Steyn
text: Well, good for you.

speaker: Mark Steyn
text: I’ll sign that petition.

speaker: Simon Schama
text: I’ll sign you up, yes.

speaker: Rudyard Griffiths
text: I want to move on to numbers, because that’s a big part of this debate.

speaker: Rudyard Griffiths
text: Turkey has 2.7 million Syrian refugees; Lebanon has a million.

speaker: Rudyard Griffiths
text: Nigel, if you look at Great Britain in terms of legally settled Syrian refugees, we’re talking almost infinitesimal numbers compared to your European counterparts.

speaker: Rudyard Griffiths
text: What do Britain, Canada, and the United States owe their European allies in terms of trying to relieve the pressure that you and Mark have diagnosed so acutely within their societies right now?

speaker: Rudyard Griffiths
text: What do we owe them?

speaker: Nigel Farage
text: We have a newfound problem in the United Kingdom with this because we have an open door to half a billion people who are European Union citizens.

speaker: Nigel Farage
text: As a result of that and generally a pretty weak U.K. immigration policy, net migration to Britain is running at a third of a million a year.

speaker: Nigel Farage
text: That’s if you believe the figures, which I really honestly don’t.

speaker: Nigel Farage
text: So our population is increasing by a third of a million every year, ten times the postwar average.

speaker: Nigel Farage
text: As a result, David Cameron has said he’s going to accept twenty thousand Syrian refugees over the course of this parliament.

speaker: Nigel Farage
text: I’m absolutely certain that if the United Kingdom had an Australian-style point system for immigration and we had net immigration running at average postwar levels of thirty thousand a year, we’d find room for some more genuine refugees.

speaker: Nigel Farage
text: And I hope that when we did, we’d look at the plight of the Christians who are being massacred in Libya, Iraq, and Syria.

speaker: Nigel Farage
text: Based on every definition that the United Nations has stood for since 1951, those Christians should be guaranteed freedom, security, and refugee status in the West.

speaker: Nigel Farage
text: I think Britain, Germany, and Sweden are actually becoming very hard-hearted because of the free movement of people.

speaker: Nigel Farage
text: We’re becoming rather hard-hearted to things that twenty years ago we’d have been happy to accept.

speaker: Rudyard Griffiths
text: Mark, the United States has a population of over 300 million, but only twelve hundred Syrian refugees have been legally and officially admitted into the country.

speaker: Rudyard Griffiths
text: Is the United States shouldering its burden of this crisis?

speaker: Mark Steyn
text: No, but they don’t look at it from a humanitarian perspective on principle.

speaker: Mark Steyn
text: They see it as part of the big security picture.

speaker: Mark Steyn
text: And it’s a little surreal to be holding this debate in the week following Brussels.

speaker: Mark Steyn
text: Louise and Simon, I think, want to detach the general migration question from the terrorism question, and the Americans don’t see it that way.

speaker: Mark Steyn
text: I was glad to hear that the zealots of Canadian customs turned Simon over at Pearson earlier today.

speaker: Mark Steyn
text: It’s good to know there’s always someone they don’t want to let in the country!

speaker: Mark Steyn
text: Immigration minister John McCallum is going to say, “We’re not going to have the chaps committing the gang rapes. No, we’re screening for them,” but if you have ever had the pleasure of undergoing so-called secondary interrogation, as this suspicious character did earlier today, you will know that no Western government has a clue about who it lets in.

speaker: Mark Steyn
text: The person who committed the San Bernardino crime had a green card.

speaker: Mark Steyn
text: She basically used a jihadist dating site to put together a terrorist cell.

speaker: Mark Steyn
text: It was an arranged marriage for the purpose of committing terrorism.

speaker: Mark Steyn
text: And she aced some sort of immigration test.

speaker: Mark Steyn
text: It’s all “money is no object” down south.

speaker: Mark Steyn
text: It’s not like here, where there’s just one little agency dealing with it: the Canada Border Services Agency.

speaker: Mark Steyn
text: They’ve got something like ninety-seven agencies south of the border looking at this woman.

speaker: Mark Steyn
text: She aced five separate tests and she still got into the country.

speaker: Mark Steyn
text: America takes the view that it has no idea who any of these people are and it’s better to be safe than sorry.

speaker: Rudyard Griffiths
text: Let’s come back now to you, Louise.

speaker: Rudyard Griffiths
text: What do Canada and the United States owe in terms of their share of this crisis?

speaker: Louise Arbour
text: I think we have to bring this debate a little bit back into a less apocalyptic scale.

speaker: Louise Arbour
text: As I said at the beginning, the wording of the motion was a poetic way of capturing the spirit and the letter of the Refugee Convention.

speaker: Louise Arbour
text: Now I think we’ve drifted into the movement of people who in fact are, for the most part, unregulated by international law or international treaty.

speaker: Louise Arbour
text: What we’re talking about now — this so-called huge crisis facing Europe — is very well defined by the Refugee Convention.

speaker: Louise Arbour
text: But we haven’t made a dent in talking about the millions of stateless people in the world who don’t have a passport.

speaker: Louise Arbour
text: And by the way, Mark, if you have a Canadian passport you’re a Canadian citizen.

speaker: Louise Arbour
text: There’s no arguing with that, right?

speaker: Louise Arbour
text: We haven’t made a dent in dealing with statelessness.

speaker: Louise Arbour
text: We haven’t made a dent in talking about what are called IDPs, internally displaced persons, of which there are millions in Syria itself and in Sudan.

speaker: Louise Arbour
text: These people are stuck in their own country against a predatory government.

speaker: Louise Arbour
text: We have no framework to deal with them and to help them.

speaker: Louise Arbour
text: What we’re talking about are people running away from oppression.

speaker: Louise Arbour
text: And frankly, when you consider the immense risks they’re taking to flee, we have to assume that at least the majority of them are bona fide refugee applicants.

speaker: Louise Arbour
text: We simply have to process them.

speaker: Louise Arbour
text: We’re talking about very small numbers.

speaker: Louise Arbour
text: Put millions into context: it’s millions of refugees knocking on the door of a billion people, if you put Europe, North America, and all the capacity of the world’s wealthy nations together.

speaker: Louise Arbour
text: The key, I believe, is international co-operation.

speaker: Louise Arbour
text: There’s no reason Greece, which was having a lot of financial problems itself, should have been stuck with bearing the largest burden.

speaker: Louise Arbour
text: The European partners, and the Western countries generally, should have stepped up to the plate.

speaker: Louise Arbour
text: I think Canada should still do so beyond the already generous signal that we have sent.

speaker: Louise Arbour
text: We have the luxury in Canada of doing a full pre-screening.

speaker: Louise Arbour
text: People don’t row into Canada.

speaker: Louise Arbour
text: They sit in refugee camps where we have months and months of pre-selection processes through the UNHCR.

speaker: Louise Arbour
text: With the luxury of these processes in place, we should be doing tons more, but that would require everyone to work in that direction and stop exaggerating.

speaker: Louise Arbour
text: I’m not saying there are zero security risks.

speaker: Louise Arbour
text: But I think it will be a stain and a shame on our generation if our response is to blow it up to such an extent that we start talking about erecting walls with barbed wires.

speaker: Rudyard Griffiths
text: We’re coming to the end of our cross-examination period, but Simon, I want to give you the last word in this segment before we go into closing statements.

speaker: Simon Schama
text: I just really want to echo what Louise has said and quickly mention a piece of information that came out today in a report from Amnesty International.

speaker: Simon Schama
text: It casts a very long shadow over the Turkey-EU agreement, if that’s going to happen.

speaker: Simon Schama
text: This very, very credible report states that Turkey has been forcibly deporting Syrian refugees back to the war zones from which they have come, which is a horrific thing to contemplate if it is true.

speaker: Simon Schama
text: The Turks have denied it, but there seems to be a very substantial amount of evidence to suggest the claims are correct.

speaker: Simon Schama
text: It throws the issue back to the place that we should have perhaps spent more time on, as Louise suggested.

speaker: Simon Schama
text: There is this kind of universe of misery and suffering, especially considering that one in every three displaced persons in these hellish camps in Syria, some in Jordan and Lebanon, are children, and we have to really think about their plight rather than obsess quite so much on jihadists and rapists in German cities.

speaker: Rudyard Griffiths
text: Very good.

speaker: Rudyard Griffiths
text: It’s time now for closing statements.

speaker: Rudyard Griffiths
text: We’re going to proceed in the opposite order of our opening statements.

speaker: Rudyard Griffiths
text: So Nigel, your three minutes will go up on the clock and you have a say.

speaker: Nigel Farage
text: Well, thank you.

speaker: Nigel Farage
text: And thank you for a very civilized debate.

speaker: Nigel Farage
text: We started off with 77 percent against our side of the argument, which, compared to the odds I’m against when I’m in the European Parliament, strikes me as being quite a good start.

speaker: Nigel Farage
text: I’ve tried to make the point that I do think it’s beholden upon people in the West to open their hearts to genuine refugees, people who live in fear of direct persecution, imprisonment, and death because of their race, religion, political beliefs, and indeed, sexual orientation.

speaker: Nigel Farage
text: I’ve tried to make that point, and I also have no doubt that America and Canada could do an awful lot more than they’re doing when it comes to refugees.

speaker: Nigel Farage
text: But it’s Europe that has faced the front line of this issue over the course of the last eighteen months, and we have thrown out of the window our classical definition of what a refugee is and broadened it to include anybody coming from a war-torn area or, frankly, anybody coming from a poor country.

speaker: Nigel Farage
text: What Chancellor Merkel did clearly was irresponsible, damn stupid, and will cost Germany for many years to come.

speaker: Nigel Farage
text: In the modern world we do have a genuine terrorist threat.

speaker: Nigel Farage
text: It’s likely that we only need to be concerned about 3 percent of the Muslim communities that are coming into Europe, but if only eight people can cause all that misery we saw in Paris, and half a dozen can do what we saw in Brussels, we have to be careful.

speaker: Nigel Farage
text: We need security checks.

speaker: Nigel Farage
text: We have to process people offshore and make sure they’re genuine refugees.

speaker: Nigel Farage
text: And I’ve tried this evening to challenge the other side to see whether they would agree with me that the Christians who are being crucified and massacred in the Middle East should qualify for refugee status and I’ve not had one positive response from them on this at all.

speaker: Nigel Farage
text: And this, ladies and gentlemen, is the point.

speaker: Nigel Farage
text: You cannot support this motion.

speaker: Nigel Farage
text: It is idealized nonsense.

speaker: Nigel Farage
text: It doesn’t make sense.

speaker: Nigel Farage
text: What we need to have is a sensible, proper, common sense refugee policy to help those who are in peril.

speaker: Nigel Farage
text: To open up our doors the way Angela Merkel did is bad news for Germany and is bad news for the West.

speaker: Nigel Farage
text: Stand up and stop such nonsense and oppose the motion, please.

speaker: Nigel Farage
text: Thank you.

speaker: Simon Schama
text: I want to say I don’t disagree at all with your point about the Christian community.

speaker: Simon Schama
text: The same goes for the Yazidis and Shia Muslims.

speaker: Simon Schama
text: As far as ISIL is concerned, Shias aren’t Muslim at all.

speaker: Simon Schama
text: I want to end with the words of a Christian, not mine, written in 1624.

speaker: Simon Schama
text: You’ll all know some of them at least, I’m sure.

speaker: Simon Schama
text: They are from the Dean of St. Paul’s, John Donne: “No man is an island entire of itself; every man is a piece of the continent, a part of the main; if a clod be washed away by the sea, Europe is the less, as well as if a promontory were, as well as any manner of thy friends or of thine own were; any man’s death diminishes me, because I am involved in mankind. And therefore never send to know for whom the bell tolls; it tolls for thee.”

speaker: Rudyard Griffiths
text: Louise, we’re going to go to Mark first, and then you’ll get the last word.

speaker: Rudyard Griffiths
text: Mark.

speaker: Mark Steyn
text: Those of us on stage and many of the more distinguished persons in the auditorium tonight lead privileged lives.

speaker: Mark Steyn
text: We jet off to the European Parliament in Strasbourg or to BBC television studios or to the transnational bureaucracy in Geneva, and from thirty-thousand feet it’s easy to think that what’s going on below us is swell.

speaker: Mark Steyn
text: We will never have to live in Molenbeek in Brussels or Rosengård in Malmö.

speaker: Mark Steyn
text: We will never have to live in Bradford or Toulouse.

speaker: Mark Steyn
text: We get to go to the nice places.

speaker: Mark Steyn
text: And that should imbue us with a certain modesty when we come up with grand, utopian schemes that testify to what Simon called our naively optimistic humanism.

speaker: Mark Steyn
text: Down there in Molenbeek and in Rosengård they have to live with the consequences of our naively optimistic humanism.

speaker: Mark Steyn
text: We are striking attitudes.

speaker: Mark Steyn
text: Simon spoke earlier about his Kurdish newsagent who’s always a very decent chap when he hands him the Jewish Chronicle in the morning.

speaker: Mark Steyn
text: We all know people like that.

speaker: Mark Steyn
text: But at the same time, the political class is designing a solution to the great migrations of the world that will only end in tragedy, and I ask you not to vote for it.

speaker: Mark Steyn
text: The more failed states that stay that way will only lead to more failed states in the future.

speaker: Mark Steyn
text: Ultimately, it is better for Syrians to be able to live in Syria, for Afghans to be able to live in Afghanistan, and for Iraqis to be able to live in Iraq.

speaker: Mark Steyn
text: The more beacons of liberty around the world the better.

speaker: Mark Steyn
text: I confess: I’ve never liked the Emma Lazarus poem that is stapled to the bottom of the Statue of Liberty.

speaker: Mark Steyn
text: The French gave the Americans a fabulous statute and the Americans nailed a third-rate poem to it and turned it into a celebration of mass migration.

speaker: Mark Steyn
text: Liberty and mass migration have nothing to do with each other, and often, the latter can imperil the former, which is where Simon’s naively optimistic humanism may take us.

speaker: Mark Steyn
text: We cannot fix failed states by inviting millions of their people to move in with us.

speaker: Mark Steyn
text: All that ensures is more failed states and more disappointment.

speaker: Mark Steyn
text: Eventually, one by one, the nations of the West will join them, and then you’ll really be yearning to breathe free and there’ll be nowhere to do it.

speaker: Mark Steyn
text: Please vote against this motion.

speaker: Rudyard Griffiths
text: Ms. Arbour, you’ll have the last word.

speaker: Louise Arbour
text: Let me say at the outset that I don’t know of any evidence that suggests that Christians from Syria, or the Druze, or the Alawites, have been excluded from refugee protection.

speaker: Louise Arbour
text: I don’t know where this is all coming from.

speaker: Louise Arbour
text: What is being portrayed as a unique case in this debate tonight is in fact just another manifestation of the old myths, stereotypes, and prejudices that have met virtually every wave of immigration, and it’s particularly odious when it targets refugees, not just any other kind of migrants.

speaker: Louise Arbour
text: In fact, Doug Saunders in his book and in a piece that he wrote in the Globe and Mail made the point that many of the things that we hear today about Muslim refugees penetrating our Western societies with a fifth column intent on destroying it were also attributed, sometimes in relatively recent parts of our histories, to Catholics.

speaker: Louise Arbour
text: For instance, they were said to be backwards and believed to have a loyalty to Rome more than to their home country; they lived in poor, crime-ridden neighbourhoods; and they were considered anti-democratic, authoritarian by disposition.

speaker: Louise Arbour
text: Doesn’t that sound also like the yellow peril?

speaker: Louise Arbour
text: People thought we were all going to be transformed into a different society, and that we’d all end up being a mixed colour if we let in these millions of people from all over the world.

speaker: Louise Arbour
text: This plays into exactly the same stereotypes and myths that we’ve heard at every single point in history.

speaker: Louise Arbour
text: The reality is that, despite an original knee-jerk, at times very hostile reception to newcomers, the history in this country has been a history of immense success of integrating people coming from all kinds of different cultures and religion.

speaker: Louise Arbour
text: And integration is a two-way street.

speaker: Louise Arbour
text: It has changed us historically and will change us in the future.

speaker: Louise Arbour
text: We must have a very impoverished confidence in our democracy to think that it is so fragile that it cannot sustain the profound differences that will challenge our devotion to free speech, freedom of assembly, and pluralism.

speaker: Louise Arbour
text: Thank you.

speaker: Rudyard Griffiths
text: Well, ladies and gentlemen, it was a hard-fought debate tonight, which brings to mind something that our founder, Peter Munk, has said on many occasions: it’s one thing to get up, give a speech, and have the stage for forty-five minutes or an hour, but what we’ve seen tonight is something very different.

speaker: Rudyard Griffiths
text: Four big thinkers challenged each other, put their ideas out there, and contested this important issue.

speaker: Rudyard Griffiths
text: So please join me in a show of appreciation for a phenomenal debate.

speaker: Rudyard Griffiths
text: Very well done, and thank you.

speaker: Rudyard Griffiths
text: Let’s take a look at where public opinion was in this hall at the beginning of the evening: 77 percent of you agreed with the motion and 23 percent were opposed.

speaker: Rudyard Griffiths
text: Then we asked how many of you would be open to changing your mind, and 79 percent said you would be.

speaker: Rudyard Griffiths
text: It’s going to be fascinating to see how all of you vote now based on what you’ve heard tonight from the “pro” and “con” sides.

speaker: Rudyard Griffiths
text: I want to end by thanking the Aurea Foundation again for staging these phenomenal debates.

speaker: Rudyard Griffiths
text: They’re a great addition to the city and to the country, and this evening has been available to people from coast to coast in Canada and across the continental United States.

speaker: Rudyard Griffiths
text: We’re going to do this all again next autumn, but in the meantime keep watching, keep learning, and keep reading.

speaker: Rudyard Griffiths
text: Thank you for joining us at the Munk Debates.

speaker: Rudyard Griffiths
text: Summary: The pre-debate vote was 77 percent in favour of the resolution, 23 percent against it.

speaker: Rudyard Griffiths
text: The final vote showed 55 percent in favour of the motion and 45 percent against.

speaker: Rudyard Griffiths
text: Given that more of the voters shifted to the team against the resolution, the victory goes to Nigel Farage and Mark Steyn.
